cards.q: What forms the continuous structural framework of the plasma membrane?
cards.a: A phospholipid bilayer.
options: A phospholipid bilayer
A sheet of cholesterol molecules
A woven network of peripheral proteins
A surface layer of membrane carbohydrate
cards.explanation: The bilayer of phospholipids is the one component that is continuous around the whole cell, and it is what makes the membrane a barrier to water soluble substances. Cholesterol is inserted between phospholipids and does not form a sheet of its own. Peripheral proteins sit on the surfaces and can be removed without opening the cell. Membrane carbohydrate is attached to lipids and proteins on the outer face only, so it cannot be the framework.

cards.q: In an intact plasma membrane, where do the fatty acid tails of the phospholipids sit?
cards.a: Facing each other in the interior of the bilayer, away from water.
options: Facing the cytosol on both leaflets
Facing each other in the interior of the bilayer, away from water
Facing the extracellular fluid on both leaflets
Alternating with the phosphate heads along each membrane surface
cards.explanation: The tails are nonpolar, so water drives them together into the core of the membrane while the polar heads face the watery fluid on each side. Tails cannot face the cytosol or the extracellular fluid, because both are water and the tails are excluded from water. Tails do not alternate with the heads along the surface, because each phospholipid keeps its head at the surface and its tails pointing inward.

cards.q: Calling a phospholipid amphipathic means that one molecule has which combination?
cards.a: A polar head that interacts with water and nonpolar tails that do not.
options: Two polar ends separated by a neutral middle
A charged head and a charged tail, both attracted to water
A polar head that interacts with water and nonpolar tails that do not
A nonpolar head and polar tails that face the cytosol
cards.explanation: Amphipathic means one molecule carries both a water loving and a water avoiding region, and that split is exactly what makes a bilayer form spontaneously. A molecule polar at both ends would dissolve rather than assemble into a sheet. A fully charged molecule would stay in solution. The head is the polar end and the tails are the nonpolar end, not the reverse.

cards.q: Which class of membrane protein extends completely through the bilayer and touches both the cytosol and the extracellular fluid?
cards.a: Integral transmembrane proteins.
options: Peripheral proteins bound to one membrane surface
Lipid anchored proteins tethered to a single leaflet
Secreted proteins that rest in the glycocalyx
Integral transmembrane proteins
cards.explanation: Only a transmembrane protein has a hydrophobic stretch long enough to cross the lipid core, which is what lets channels and transporters connect the two sides of the cell. Peripheral proteins bind to a surface and never enter the core. Lipid anchored proteins are attached to a fatty acid in one leaflet and stay on that side. Secreted proteins are outside the membrane entirely.

cards.q: How is cholesterol positioned within the plasma membrane?
cards.a: Wedged between phospholipids, with its hydroxyl group near the polar heads and its rings among the tails.
options: Wedged between phospholipids, with its hydroxyl near the polar heads
Floating free in the cytosol just under the inner leaflet
Coating the outer surface as a continuous waterproof film
Packed in the center of the bilayer with no contact with the heads
cards.explanation: Cholesterol is itself amphipathic, so its single hydroxyl group sits with the polar heads while its stiff ring structure sits among the fatty acid tails, and that position is what lets it control packing. Cytosolic cholesterol would not affect membrane fluidity. A surface film would block the transport proteins. Burying it entirely in the center would leave the hydroxyl group in the hydrophobic core, which it avoids.

cards.q: On which face of the plasma membrane are the carbohydrate chains of glycolipids and glycoproteins found?
cards.a: Only on the extracellular face.
options: Only on the cytosolic face
Only on the extracellular face
Equally on both faces
Buried inside the hydrophobic core
cards.explanation: Carbohydrate is added in the endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi on the side of the membrane that becomes the outside, so the sugar coat always ends up facing the extracellular fluid where recognition happens. A cytosolic sugar coat would be useless for cell to cell identification. The asymmetry is maintained, so the two faces are not alike. Carbohydrate is strongly polar and cannot sit in the lipid core.

cards.q: Which membrane proteins can be released by changing the pH or salt concentration of the surrounding solution, without breaking up the bilayer?
cards.a: Peripheral proteins, which are attached to a membrane surface.
options: Integral proteins that span the lipid core
Lipid anchored proteins covalently attached to a fatty acid
Peripheral proteins attached to a membrane surface
Glycoproteins with carbohydrate on the outer face
cards.explanation: Peripheral proteins are held on by ionic and hydrogen bonds to lipid heads or to other proteins, and those bonds are exactly what salt and pH changes disrupt. Integral proteins are held by hydrophobic contact with the lipid core, so they come out only when detergent breaks the bilayer. A lipid anchor is a covalent bond and is not undone by salt. Glycoproteins are typically integral proteins and stay put for the same reason.

cards.q: What holds a phospholipid bilayer together?
cards.a: Hydrophobic interaction among the fatty acid tails, together with attraction of the polar heads to water.
options: Covalent bonds linking each phospholipid to its neighbors
Disulfide bridges between the embedded membrane proteins
Hydrogen bonds formed directly between the fatty acid tails
Hydrophobic interaction among the fatty acid tails
cards.explanation: The bilayer is held by weak, noncovalent forces, mainly the tendency of the nonpolar tails to cluster away from water while the polar heads stay in it, which is why the membrane can self seal and why its parts can move sideways. Covalent bonds between phospholipids would lock the membrane rigid and prevent that movement. Disulfide bridges stabilize some proteins but do not build the lipid sheet. Fatty acid tails are nonpolar and cannot form hydrogen bonds.

cards.q: A membrane rich in cholesterol is cooled from 37 C to 20 C. Compared with the same membrane without cholesterol, what happens to its fluidity?
cards.a: It stays more fluid, because cholesterol keeps the phospholipids from packing tightly.
options: It stays more fluid, because cholesterol blocks tight packing of the tails
It becomes far more rigid, because cholesterol crystallizes with the tails
It is unchanged, because cholesterol acts only on the outer leaflet
It becomes completely liquid, because cholesterol dissolves the bilayer
cards.explanation: At low temperature the danger is that tails pack together and the membrane gels, and the bulky cholesterol ring gets in the way of that packing. Cholesterol does the opposite job at high temperature, where it restrains movement and reduces fluidity, so its effect depends on where you start. Cholesterol is present in both leaflets, not just the outer one. It never dissolves the membrane, since it is a structural part of it.

cards.q: Two membranes are compared at 37 C. Membrane A has mostly saturated fatty acid tails and membrane B has mostly unsaturated tails. Which is more fluid?
cards.a: Membrane B, because kinks at the double bonds prevent the tails from packing closely.
options: Membrane A, because straight tails slide past each other easily
Membrane B, because kinks at the double bonds prevent close packing
Both are the same, because fluidity depends only on temperature
Membrane A, because saturated tails carry more cholesterol
cards.explanation: Every double bond puts a bend in the tail, so neighboring phospholipids cannot line up closely and the membrane stays loose and mobile. Straight saturated tails do the opposite, stacking neatly and stiffening the membrane. Temperature matters, but composition changes fluidity at any given temperature. Saturation does not determine how much cholesterol a membrane holds.

cards.q: A treatment makes a cell membrane much less fluid at body temperature. What happens to the rate of carrier mediated transport across it?
cards.a: It falls, because carriers must change shape within the bilayer to move solute.
options: It rises, because a stiffer membrane holds carriers in the open position
It is unchanged, because carriers work independently of the lipid around them
It falls, because carrier proteins must change conformation inside the bilayer
It rises, because a rigid membrane brings carriers closer to their solute
cards.explanation: A carrier binds solute on one side, changes shape, and releases it on the other, and that shape change is resisted when the surrounding lipid is stiff. A rigid membrane does not lock carriers open, since the carrier cycles between two shapes and needs both. Carriers are embedded in lipid and are very much affected by it. Rigidity does not shorten the distance between carrier and solute, which is set by the fluid on each side.

cards.q: A membrane protein can be released only by adding a detergent that breaks up the bilayer. What does that tell you about the protein?
cards.a: It has a hydrophobic region buried in the lipid core, so it is an integral protein.
options: It is held to the surface by ionic bonds, so it is a peripheral protein
It is a carbohydrate rich protein of the glycocalyx
It is a cytosolic protein that was contaminating the sample
It has a hydrophobic region in the lipid core, so it is an integral protein
cards.explanation: Detergent is needed only when the protein is held by hydrophobic contact with the fatty acid tails, which is the defining feature of an integral protein. A peripheral protein would have come off with a simple change in salt or pH. Glycocalyx carbohydrate faces the watery outside and does not require detergent to reach. A cytosolic contaminant would appear in the first wash, before any detergent was used.

cards.q: An enzyme strips the carbohydrate chains from the outer surface of a cell but leaves the bilayer intact. Which function is most directly lost?
cards.a: Recognition of the cell by other cells and by immune proteins.
options: Recognition of the cell by other cells and by immune proteins
The barrier that keeps Na+ from leaking into the cell
The ability of the membrane to reseal after a small tear
The attraction between the phosphate heads and water
cards.explanation: The sugar coat is the cell's identity tag, so removing it interferes with recognition, adhesion, and immune identification while leaving the lipid seal untouched. The barrier to Na+ is a property of the hydrophobic core, which the enzyme never touches. Resealing is also a lipid property and is preserved. The phosphate heads are still polar and still face water after the sugars are gone.

cards.q: A labeled phospholipid in the outer leaflet spreads sideways across the cell surface within seconds but takes hours to show up in the inner leaflet. What explains the difference?
cards.a: Sideways movement is easy, but flipping requires dragging the polar head through the hydrophobic core.
options: The inner leaflet contains no phospholipid for the label to mix with
Sideways movement is easy, but flipping drags the head through the core
The label is destroyed by cytosolic enzymes as soon as it flips
Sideways movement uses ATP while flipping does not
cards.explanation: Lateral diffusion keeps each polar head in water the whole time, so it costs almost nothing, while a flip forces that head through the greasy core and is energetically expensive. The inner leaflet is also phospholipid, so there is plenty for the label to join. Destruction of the label would remove signal rather than delay it. Lateral diffusion is passive, and it is the flip that cells must speed up with ATP driven flippases.

cards.q: A membrane sample turns out to be about 75 percent protein by mass, far above the usual value. What does that suggest about the membrane?
cards.a: It carries out a great deal of transport and signaling work.
options: It is a poor barrier to water because protein has replaced the lipid seal
It has lost its cholesterol and has become unusually rigid
It carries out a great deal of transport and signaling work
It is an inactive storage membrane with little traffic across it
cards.explanation: Proteins are the working parts of a membrane, so a high protein fraction points to heavy transport, enzyme, or signaling activity, as seen in the inner mitochondrial membrane. The lipid bilayer is still continuous around the proteins, so the barrier remains intact. Protein content says nothing directly about cholesterol content or rigidity. A quiet storage membrane would be the low protein case, such as the myelin sheath.

cards.q: A drug removes most of the cholesterol from the plasma membrane of a cell held at 37 C. Follow the consequence through: what happens to fluidity, and then to the passive leak of small solutes?
cards.a: Fluidity rises and the passive leak increases, so the pumps must work harder to hold the gradients.
options: Fluidity falls and passive leak falls, so pumps can slow down
Fluidity rises but leak is unchanged, because leak depends only on protein channels
Fluidity is unchanged, because cholesterol affects only membrane thickness
Fluidity rises and passive leak increases, so pumps must work harder to hold gradients
cards.explanation: At body temperature cholesterol restrains the tails, so taking it away loosens the packing, and a looser core lets small solutes and water slip through more easily. The pumps then run faster and burn more ATP to keep the same gradients. Losing cholesterol at 37 C increases fluidity rather than decreasing it. Leak is not purely a channel property, since the lipid core itself has a measurable permeability that packing controls.

cards.q: A bacterium is moved from 37 C to 20 C but is genetically unable to change its fatty acid composition. Predict the state of its membrane and the effect on nutrient uptake.
cards.a: The membrane stiffens toward a gel and carrier mediated uptake slows.
options: The membrane stiffens toward a gel and carrier mediated uptake slows
The membrane becomes more fluid and uptake speeds up
The membrane is unaffected because bilayers are temperature independent
The membrane ruptures immediately because cold expands the bilayer
cards.explanation: Cooling lets the tails pack closer, and a cell that cannot add unsaturated tails or cholesterol has no way to counter it, so the membrane approaches a gel state. Carriers and pumps must flex to work, so their turnover falls and nutrients enter more slowly. Cooling reduces fluidity rather than increasing it. Bilayers do not rupture on cooling, they gel, and it is warming that eventually disorders them.

cards.q: A newly sequenced membrane protein contains one stretch of about 20 hydrophobic amino acids flanked on both sides by charged residues. Where does that stretch sit, and what does the arrangement let the protein do?
cards.a: It spans the bilayer once, so the protein can connect events outside the cell to events inside.
options: It lies flat on the outer surface, so the protein can bind sugars
It spans the bilayer once, so the protein can link the outside to the inside
It coils inside the cytosol, so the protein can bind ATP
It is cleaved off in the Golgi, so the mature protein is secreted
cards.explanation: A run of about 20 hydrophobic residues is the right length to cross the lipid core, and charged residues at both ends anchor it at the two watery surfaces, which is the signature of a single pass transmembrane protein. That geometry is what lets a receptor bind a messenger outside and change something inside. A surface protein would not need a long hydrophobic run at all. A cytosolic domain would be flanked by cytosol on both sides, not by the membrane, and a cleaved signal sequence would leave no membrane anchor behind.

cards.q: A cell is treated so that the carbohydrate of its glycocalyx is destroyed while the bilayer stays intact. Predict what happens to its permeability barrier and to its recognition by immune cells.
cards.a: The barrier is preserved but immune recognition is disturbed.
options: Both the barrier and recognition fail, since carbohydrate seals the membrane
The barrier fails but recognition is preserved, since sugars are only structural
The barrier is preserved but immune recognition is disturbed
Neither changes, since carbohydrate has no physiological role
cards.explanation: Sealing and recognition are done by different parts of the membrane, so this experiment separates them cleanly: the hydrophobic core still blocks ions and polar solutes, while the missing sugar coat is exactly what immune cells and neighboring cells read. Carbohydrate contributes nothing to the seal, so the barrier cannot fail here. Recognition cannot be preserved, because the surface markers are the thing that was destroyed. Blood group antigens are membrane carbohydrate, so the role is real and physiologically important.

cards.q: Which substance crosses a pure lipid bilayer most readily without help from a protein?
cards.a: Oxygen.
options: Sodium ion
Glucose
Chloride ion
Oxygen
cards.explanation: Oxygen is small and nonpolar, so it dissolves in the fatty acid core and passes straight through. Na+ and Cl- are charged and carry a shell of water, which the hydrophobic core will not admit, so both need channels. Glucose is uncharged but large and heavily hydroxylated, so it needs a transporter such as GLUT.

cards.q: Which property of a molecule most increases its ability to cross a lipid bilayer unaided?
cards.a: High lipid solubility.
options: High lipid solubility
A large net negative charge
A high molecular weight
A large shell of bound water
cards.explanation: Crossing the membrane means dissolving into the fatty acid core and out again, so the more lipid soluble a molecule is, the faster it goes. Net charge does the opposite, since the nonpolar core repels charged particles. High molecular weight slows a molecule down at any given lipid solubility. A shell of bound water makes the effective particle much larger and more polar, which also slows crossing.

cards.q: Why do charged particles cross the lipid core of a membrane so poorly?
cards.a: The nonpolar core will not accept a charge or the water shell that travels with it.
options: They are all too large to fit between the phospholipids
The nonpolar core will not accept a charge or its water shell
They are repelled by the carbohydrate on the outer face
They bind irreversibly to cholesterol in the bilayer
cards.explanation: Stripping the water from an ion and pushing the bare charge into a greasy interior costs far more energy than an ion has at body temperature, so ions travel through protein channels instead. Size is not the problem, since ions like Na+ are far smaller than steroids that cross easily. The surface carbohydrate is a thin polar coat and does not repel ions. Ions do not bind cholesterol.

cards.q: How does most water actually cross the plasma membrane of a cell that needs high water permeability?
cards.a: Through aquaporin channels.
options: By dissolving freely in the fatty acid core
By being pumped across using ATP
Through aquaporin channels
Bound to glucose on a shared transporter
cards.explanation: Water is small but polar, so a little crosses the lipid directly, and cells that must move a lot of water insert aquaporins to speed it up. Water is not lipid soluble, so free dissolution in the core is slow, not free. There is no ATP driven water pump in human cells, since water follows osmotic gradients instead. Water is not carried piggyback on the glucose transporter.

cards.q: Which of these substances requires a membrane protein in order to enter a cell at a useful rate?
cards.a: Glucose.
options: Carbon dioxide
Oxygen
A steroid hormone
Glucose
cards.explanation: Glucose is a fairly large polar molecule with many hydroxyl groups, so it needs a GLUT carrier or a sodium coupled transporter to move at physiological speed. CO2 and O2 are small nonpolar gases that dissolve in lipid and diffuse straight through. Steroid hormones are lipid derived and cross so freely that their receptors sit inside the cell.

cards.q: Steroid hormones cross the plasma membrane without a transporter mainly because they are what?
cards.a: Lipid soluble.
options: Lipid soluble
Very small and positively charged
Bound to plasma albumin
Broken down into amino acids first
cards.explanation: Steroids are made from cholesterol and dissolve readily in the membrane core, which is why their receptors are cytosolic or nuclear rather than on the surface. They are not small ions and carry no useful charge. Binding to albumin keeps a steroid in the blood, and it is the free fraction that crosses. Steroids are not proteins and are not digested into amino acids.

cards.q: Two molecules are equally lipid soluble but one is much larger. How do their rates of simple diffusion across a bilayer compare?
cards.a: The smaller one crosses faster.
options: The larger one crosses faster
The smaller one crosses faster
They cross at the same rate, since only lipid solubility matters
Neither crosses, since size blocks all simple diffusion
cards.explanation: Size and lipid solubility both matter, and when lipid solubility is held equal, the smaller molecule slips between the fatty acid tails more easily and diffuses faster. Larger molecules must push more tails apart, which slows them. Lipid solubility alone does not determine rate. Size slows diffusion but does not abolish it, as fairly large steroids still cross.

cards.q: What does it mean to call the plasma membrane selectively permeable?
cards.a: It lets some substances cross while restricting others.
options: It blocks every substance until a pump is activated
It allows anything smaller than a protein to pass freely
It lets some substances cross while restricting others
It allows movement in one direction only
cards.explanation: Selective permeability is the basis of every gradient in the body, because the membrane admits gases and lipid soluble molecules while holding back ions and large polar solutes. A membrane that blocked everything would not allow O2 uptake, which happens with no pump at all. Size is not the only filter, since small ions are blocked while much larger steroids pass. Simple diffusion has no built in direction, since it follows whichever gradient exists.

cards.q: A new drug is small, uncharged, and highly lipid soluble. What do you predict about how it enters cells?
cards.a: It diffuses straight through the bilayer without a transporter.
options: It needs a specific carrier protein and will saturate at high dose
It enters only by ATP driven pumping
It cannot enter cells and stays in the extracellular fluid
It diffuses straight through the bilayer without a transporter
cards.explanation: Small, uncharged, and lipid soluble is the exact profile that crosses by simple diffusion, so the rate will rise in proportion to the concentration gradient with no ceiling. A carrier would impose saturation, which simple diffusion does not show. No pump is needed for a molecule that has no charge to fight and no gradient to climb. Being lipid soluble is the opposite of being trapped outside.

cards.q: A weak acid drug exists as an uncharged molecule and as its negatively charged conjugate base. Which form crosses the lipid bilayer, and what does that mean in an acidic fluid?
cards.a: The uncharged form crosses, and acidic fluid increases the uncharged fraction so more crosses.
options: The uncharged form crosses, and acid increases the uncharged fraction so more crosses
The charged form crosses, and acid increases the charged fraction so more crosses
Both forms cross equally, so pH has no effect
Neither form crosses without a transporter, so pH is irrelevant
cards.explanation: Charge is the main obstacle to crossing lipid, so only the protonated, uncharged form of a weak acid moves through the bilayer, and adding H+ pushes the equilibrium toward that form. The charged conjugate base is held back by the hydrophobic core. The two forms are not equivalent, which is why pH shifts drug movement so strongly. A transporter is not required, because the uncharged form is lipid soluble.

cards.q: CO2 is more soluble in lipid than O2 is, and the two are similar in size. Which crosses the alveolar membrane faster for the same partial pressure difference?
cards.a: CO2, because higher lipid solubility raises the diffusion rate.
options: O2, because it is the gas the body needs more urgently
CO2, because higher lipid solubility raises the diffusion rate
They cross at identical rates, since both are gases
Neither crosses, since gases require channel proteins
cards.explanation: Diffusion rate through a bilayer depends on how well the molecule dissolves in lipid, and CO2 is roughly twenty times more soluble than O2, so it moves much faster for the same driving pressure. Physiological need does not change the physical properties of a molecule. Being a gas is not enough, since gases still differ in solubility. Gases require no channels at all, since they dissolve directly in the membrane.

cards.q: An amino acid and a similarly sized uncharged molecule are offered to a cell whose transporters are all blocked. Which enters, and why?
cards.a: The uncharged molecule, because the amino acid carries charge at body pH.
options: The amino acid, because the cell needs it to build proteins
Both equally, because the two molecules are the same size
The uncharged molecule, because the amino acid is charged at body pH
Neither, because blocking the transporters stops all entry
cards.explanation: At pH 7.4 an amino acid is a zwitterion with charged amino and carboxyl groups, so the lipid core rejects it and blocking the transporters cuts off its route entirely. The cell's need for amino acids does not create a path across the lipid. Equal size does not mean equal permeability once charge differs. Simple diffusion continues for the uncharged molecule even with every transporter blocked.

cards.q: Aquaporins are inserted into a membrane that previously had none. What changes?
cards.a: Water permeability rises sharply while solute permeability is essentially unchanged.
options: Both water and small solute permeability rise together
Water permeability rises and the cell begins to swell even in an isotonic solution
Water permeability falls, since the channels must first be activated by ATP
Water permeability rises sharply while solute permeability is essentially unchanged
cards.explanation: Aquaporins form a narrow pore that admits water in single file and excludes ions and solutes, so they change how fast water moves without changing what else can cross. They are not general pores, so solutes do not follow. Faster water movement does not by itself create swelling, because an isotonic solution offers no net driving force. Aquaporins are always open channels and do not need ATP.

cards.q: A fluorescent dye is injected into a cell and stays inside for hours. What does that tell you about the dye?
cards.a: It is polar or charged and has no transporter to carry it out.
options: It is polar or charged and has no transporter to carry it out
It is highly lipid soluble and dissolves in the membrane
It is pumped inward continuously by the Na+/K+ ATPase
It has been covalently bonded to the phospholipid tails
cards.explanation: A dye that stays put is one the bilayer will not admit and no carrier recognizes, which is exactly why polar or charged dyes are chosen for this purpose. A lipid soluble dye would leak straight back out within minutes. The Na+/K+ ATPase moves only Na+ and K+, so it cannot trap a dye. Covalent bonding to tails would place the dye in the membrane rather than in the cytosol.

cards.q: Urea is small and uncharged but polar. What does that predict about how it crosses membranes?
cards.a: It crosses the bilayer slowly on its own, and cells needing fast movement use urea transporters.
options: It crosses as fast as O2, because small uncharged molecules all behave alike
It crosses slowly on its own, and cells needing speed use urea transporters
It cannot cross at all, because polar molecules are completely excluded
It crosses only when pumped against its gradient using ATP
cards.explanation: Polarity slows urea down without stopping it, so it leaks through the lipid over minutes, and the kidney medulla adds specific urea transporters where rapid movement matters. It is far slower than O2 because O2 is nonpolar and urea is not. Complete exclusion is wrong, and the fact that urea does eventually cross is what makes it behave as a penetrating solute in tonicity problems. No ATP is needed, since urea follows its gradient.

cards.q: A weakly basic drug is uncharged in plasma at pH 7.4 but becomes protonated and charged at pH 5. Predict what happens when it reaches a lysosome with an internal pH of 5.
cards.a: It crosses in uncharged and becomes charged inside, so it is trapped and accumulates.
options: It crosses in and back out equally, so its concentration matches the cytosol
It is excluded from the lysosome, because acidic compartments repel all drugs
It crosses in uncharged and becomes charged inside, so it is trapped and accumulates
It is pumped out of the lysosome by an ATPase specific for weak bases
cards.explanation: The uncharged form is lipid soluble and crosses the lysosomal membrane freely, but as soon as it picks up a proton inside it cannot cross back, so drug piles up in the acidic compartment. This is ion trapping, and it is why some drugs concentrate hundreds of times in acidic spaces. Equal movement in both directions would require the drug to stay uncharged inside, which the low pH prevents. Nothing repels the neutral form on the way in, and no general weak base pump is doing this work.

cards.q: A local anesthetic must cross the axon membrane in its uncharged form and then block the Na+ channel from the cytosolic side in its charged form. Predict what happens when it is injected into inflamed tissue where the extracellular pH is low.
cards.a: Less drug is uncharged outside, so less enters the axon and the block is weaker.
options: More drug is uncharged outside, so entry rises and the block is stronger
Entry is unchanged, because the membrane admits both forms equally
The drug is destroyed by acid, so it has no effect at any dose
Less drug is uncharged outside, so less enters the axon and the block is weaker
cards.explanation: Low pH pushes this weak base toward its protonated, charged form, and the charged form cannot cross the lipid core, so less drug reaches the inside where it acts. Acid does not increase the neutral fraction of a base, it decreases it. The membrane strongly favors the uncharged form, which is the whole reason pH matters here. The drug is not chemically destroyed, it is simply held on the wrong side.

cards.q: A synthetic bilayer containing no proteins is placed in a solution of oxygen, urea, glucose, and Na+. After ten seconds, which appear inside, and which are still essentially outside after an hour?
cards.a: Oxygen enters at once, urea enters slowly, and glucose and Na+ do not enter at all.
options: Oxygen enters at once, urea slowly, and glucose and Na+ not at all
All four enter within seconds, since a bilayer is freely permeable
Only Na+ enters, since ions are the smallest particles present
Glucose and Na+ enter first, since the cell needs them most
cards.explanation: Ranking by charge, then polarity, then size gives the order directly: nonpolar O2 dissolves in the core at once, small polar urea trickles through, large polar glucose needs GLUT, and charged Na+ needs a channel, and this bilayer has neither. A bilayer is selectively permeable, not freely permeable. Small size does not help Na+ because its charge and water shell are the barrier. A protein free membrane has no way to sense what a cell needs.

cards.q: A cell's glucose transporters are knocked out. Predict the effect on glucose entry and on the entry of a lipid soluble vitamin.
cards.a: Glucose entry nearly stops while the vitamin still enters by simple diffusion.
options: Both stop, since all entry into cells depends on transport proteins
Glucose entry nearly stops while the vitamin still enters by simple diffusion
Glucose entry is unchanged, since glucose can dissolve in the lipid core
Vitamin entry rises to compensate for the loss of glucose uptake
cards.explanation: Glucose depends completely on carriers because it is large and polar, so losing them cuts off its route, while a lipid soluble vitamin dissolves in the membrane and never needed a protein. Not everything entering a cell needs a protein, as gases and steroids show. Glucose is far too polar to dissolve in the core at any useful rate. Simple diffusion of the vitamin is driven by its own gradient and does not speed up because glucose uptake failed.

cards.q: According to Fick's law, increasing which variable increases the rate of diffusion across a membrane?
cards.a: Surface area available for exchange.
options: Membrane thickness
Molecular weight of the diffusing substance
Surface area available for exchange
Distance between the two compartments
cards.explanation: Rate is directly proportional to surface area, because more area means more parallel routes across the barrier. Thickness sits in the denominator, so increasing it slows transfer. Larger molecules diffuse more slowly, so molecular weight also works against rate. Greater distance slows diffusion for the same reason thickness does.

cards.q: In Fick's law, the rate of diffusion is inversely proportional to which variable?
cards.a: Membrane thickness.
options: Concentration difference
Surface area
Temperature
Membrane thickness
cards.explanation: Thickness is the distance the molecule must travel, and it appears in the denominator, so doubling it halves the rate. Concentration difference is the driving force and multiplies the rate. Surface area also multiplies the rate. Warming speeds molecular motion, so temperature increases rather than decreases the rate.

cards.q: What supplies the driving force for simple diffusion across a membrane?
cards.a: The concentration gradient of the diffusing substance.
options: The concentration gradient of the diffusing substance
Hydrolysis of ATP by a membrane pump
Binding of the substance to a carrier protein
The electrical charge on the membrane carbohydrate
cards.explanation: Simple diffusion is powered by the random thermal motion of molecules plus a difference in concentration, which is why it costs the cell nothing. ATP is required for active transport, which is a different process and can move solute uphill. Carrier binding describes facilitated diffusion and active transport, not simple diffusion. Surface carbohydrate does not drive movement of neutral solutes across the bilayer.

cards.q: How does the size of a molecule affect its rate of diffusion, other things being equal?
cards.a: Larger molecules diffuse more slowly.
options: Larger molecules diffuse more quickly
Larger molecules diffuse more slowly
Size has no effect on diffusion rate
Only molecules above 100 daltons diffuse at all
cards.explanation: A larger particle moves more sluggishly at a given temperature and has more trouble pushing between the phospholipid tails, so its diffusion coefficient is smaller. Larger molecules never move faster for the same driving force. Size is one of the main determinants of the diffusion coefficient, so it cannot be ignored. There is no size threshold below which diffusion stops, since very small molecules diffuse fastest of all.

cards.q: How does the time required for a molecule to diffuse a given distance change as that distance increases?
cards.a: It increases with the square of the distance.
options: It increases in direct proportion to the distance
It decreases as distance increases
It increases with the square of the distance
It does not depend on distance
cards.explanation: Diffusion is a random walk, so doubling the distance multiplies the time by four, which is why diffusion is excellent over a few micrometers and hopeless over centimeters. Simple proportionality would make diffusion far more capable over distance than it actually is. Time cannot fall as distance rises. Distance is the single most important limit on diffusion, so it certainly matters.

cards.q: Net diffusion of a solute across a membrane stops when which condition is reached?
cards.a: The concentration is equal on both sides.
options: All molecular motion has ceased
The solute has all moved to one side
The membrane has become impermeable to the solute
The concentration is equal on both sides
cards.explanation: At equilibrium molecules still cross in both directions, but the two fluxes are equal, so there is no net movement. Molecular motion never stops at body temperature, which is what keeps the two way exchange going. Diffusion moves solute down its gradient, so it never piles everything on one side. The membrane's permeability does not change as equilibrium is approached.

cards.q: Which of these is not a variable in Fick's law of diffusion?
cards.a: The amount of ATP available to the cell.
options: The amount of ATP available to the cell
The surface area of the barrier
The thickness of the barrier
The concentration difference across the barrier
cards.explanation: Fick's law describes a passive process, so energy supply never appears in it and diffusion continues in a cell with no ATP at all. Surface area, thickness, and the concentration difference are the three variables that physiology manipulates most often, in the lung, the gut, and the capillary bed. Recognizing that ATP is absent is the fastest way to tell diffusion apart from active transport.

cards.q: How does raising the temperature affect the rate of diffusion?
cards.a: It increases the rate.
options: It decreases the rate
It increases the rate
It has no effect on the rate
It stops diffusion once the solution is warm
cards.explanation: Temperature is a measure of molecular kinetic energy, so warmer molecules move faster and spread more quickly. Cooling does the opposite and is why lab demonstrations run slowly in cold water. Temperature is one of the standard determinants of the diffusion coefficient, so it is never neutral. Nothing about warming halts diffusion.

cards.q: The surface area available for exchange doubles while everything else stays the same. What happens to the rate of diffusion?
cards.a: It doubles.
options: It halves
It quadruples
It doubles
It is unchanged
cards.explanation: Surface area is in the numerator of Fick's law and enters as a simple multiplier, so twice the area gives twice the transfer. Halving would be the answer if the thickness had doubled instead. Quadrupling would require a squared relationship, which applies to diffusion time and distance, not to area. Area is a real variable, so the rate cannot stay put.

cards.q: Fluid collects in the space between the alveolus and the capillary, doubling the distance oxygen must travel. What happens to the rate of oxygen transfer, other things equal?
cards.a: It falls to about half.
options: It doubles
It falls to about one quarter
It is unchanged, because the gradient is what matters
It falls to about half
cards.explanation: Thickness sits in the denominator of Fick's law, so doubling it cuts the transfer rate roughly in half, which is why pulmonary edema causes hypoxemia. Increasing the barrier thickness cannot increase transfer. The quarter answer would apply to the time for a molecule to random walk twice the distance, not to the steady state flux described by Fick's law. The gradient matters too, but it is not the only variable.

cards.q: The concentration difference across a membrane is tripled while area and thickness stay the same. What happens to the rate of diffusion?
cards.a: It triples.
options: It triples
It falls to one third
It is unchanged, since diffusion has a fixed maximum
It rises ninefold
cards.explanation: The concentration difference is the driving force and enters Fick's law as a direct multiplier, so three times the gradient gives three times the flux. A fall would require the gradient to be in the denominator, which it is not. Simple diffusion has no transport maximum, since there is no carrier to saturate, which is one way it differs from facilitated diffusion. Nothing in Fick's law is squared.

cards.q: Emphysema destroys alveolar walls, so many small alveoli merge into fewer large ones. Which variable of Fick's law changes, and how does gas transfer respond?
cards.a: Surface area falls, so gas transfer falls.
options: Membrane thickness falls, so gas transfer rises
Surface area falls, so gas transfer falls
The concentration gradient rises, so gas transfer rises
The diffusion coefficient of oxygen falls, so gas transfer falls
cards.explanation: Merging many small sacs into a few large ones keeps the volume but loses an enormous amount of surface, and area multiplies the transfer rate directly. Wall destruction does not usefully thin the barrier, and even if it did, the loss of area dominates. The alveolar to capillary gradient is set by ventilation and blood flow, not by wall destruction. The diffusion coefficient is a property of oxygen and the tissue, and disease does not change it.

cards.q: A cell increases in radius so that the distance from its surface to its center goes from 10 micrometers to 20 micrometers. How does the time for a solute to diffuse to the center change?
cards.a: It increases about fourfold.
options: It doubles
It is halved
It increases about fourfold
It stays the same
cards.explanation: Diffusion time rises with the square of distance, so doubling the distance multiplies the time by four, and this is the main reason cells stay small. Doubling would be the answer only if time were directly proportional to distance. Time cannot fall as the distance grows. Distance is the dominant term here, so it certainly matters.

cards.q: A diffusion demonstration is repeated at 37 C instead of 20 C. What happens to the rate at which the dye spreads?
cards.a: It increases, because molecules move faster at higher temperature.
options: It decreases, because heat drives water out of the gel
It is unchanged, because Fick's law contains no temperature term
It increases only if the gradient is also increased
It increases, because molecules move faster at higher temperature
cards.explanation: Warming raises molecular kinetic energy and therefore the diffusion coefficient, so the same gradient produces faster spread. Heat does not push the dye backward or dry the gel appreciably over a demonstration. Temperature acts through the diffusion coefficient, so it is part of the law even when written as a single constant. The gradient can stay exactly the same and the rate will still rise.

cards.q: The small intestine has villi and microvilli that raise its lining area many times over. Which term of Fick's law does this exploit, and with what result?
cards.a: It raises surface area, so the rate of nutrient absorption rises.
options: It raises surface area, so the rate of nutrient absorption rises
It lowers barrier thickness, so absorption rises
It raises the diffusion coefficient of glucose, so absorption rises
It raises the concentration gradient of nutrients, so absorption rises
cards.explanation: Folding the surface multiplies the area for exchange without needing a longer gut, and area multiplies the flux directly. The epithelium is not made thinner by folding it. The diffusion coefficient depends on the molecule and the medium and is unchanged by anatomy. The gradient is created by the meal and by transport out of the cell, not by folding.

cards.q: In a diseased lung the alveolar surface area is cut in half, but supplemental oxygen doubles the alveolar to capillary oxygen gradient. Predict the net effect on oxygen transfer.
cards.a: Transfer returns to about its original rate, since halving area and doubling gradient cancel.
options: Transfer falls to about one quarter, since both changes reduce it
Transfer returns to about its original rate, since the two changes cancel
Transfer doubles, since the gradient change outweighs the area change
Transfer stops, since area is the only variable that matters
cards.explanation: Both area and the concentration difference are multipliers in the numerator of Fick's law, so multiplying by one half and by two returns the product to where it started, which is why supplemental oxygen helps in diffusion limited disease. Only the area change reduces transfer, so the two do not compound. The gradient does not outweigh area, since the two terms carry equal weight. Area is one of several variables and never acts alone.

cards.q: A barrier becomes three times thicker while its surface area doubles. What happens to the rate of diffusion across it?
cards.a: It falls to about two thirds of the original rate.
options: It rises to about six times the original rate
It falls to about one sixth of the original rate
It falls to about two thirds of the original rate
It is unchanged, since the two effects cancel exactly
cards.explanation: Area multiplies the rate and thickness divides it, so the new rate is the old rate times two divided by three, which is about 0.67 of the original. Multiplying the two factors together would treat thickness as if it helped, which it does not. Dividing by both would treat area as if it hurt. Exact cancellation would require the two factors to be equal, and two and three are not.

cards.q: A single cell of 10 micrometers relies entirely on diffusion for oxygen. A tissue 1 centimeter thick cannot. Explain the physiological consequence of the distance rule.
cards.a: Diffusion time rises with the square of distance, so large tissues need bulk flow of blood to carry oxygen close to every cell.
options: Diffusion stops entirely beyond 100 micrometers, so deep tissue relies on anaerobic metabolism alone
Diffusion slows in direct proportion to distance, so a centimeter takes only a thousand times as long as a micrometer
Diffusion is unaffected by distance, and deep tissue hypoxia results from low capillary density alone
Diffusion time rises with the square of distance, so large tissues need blood flow to bring oxygen close to every cell
cards.explanation: Because time scales with the square of distance, moving oxygen a centimeter by diffusion would take hours, so the circulation carries it by bulk flow to within about 50 micrometers of every cell and lets diffusion cover only the last short step. Diffusion does not have a hard cutoff, it simply becomes impractically slow. Simple proportionality would badly understate the penalty of distance. Distance is precisely the variable at issue here.

cards.q: Two exchange surfaces are compared. Surface A has twice the area of B and half the thickness of B, and both face the same concentration difference. How do their diffusion rates compare?
cards.a: A transfers about four times as fast as B.
options: A transfers about four times as fast as B
A transfers about twice as fast as B
A and B transfer at the same rate
A transfers half as fast as B
cards.explanation: Doubling area multiplies the rate by two and halving thickness multiplies it by two again, so the two changes compound to a factor of four. Counting only one of the two changes gives the twofold answer. The changes both favor A, so they cannot cancel. Nothing here slows A down, so it cannot be the slower surface.

cards.q: Osmolarity measures which property of a solution?
cards.a: The total number of dissolved solute particles per liter of solution.
options: The number of particles that can cross the cell membrane
The total number of dissolved solute particles per liter of solution
The mass in grams of solute per liter of solution
The electrical charge carried by the dissolved solutes
cards.explanation: Osmolarity is a head count of particles and does not care what they are, so 300 mOsm/L of urea and 300 mOsm/L of NaCl have the same osmolarity. Counting only particles that cannot cross is tonicity, which is a different measurement. Mass per liter is concentration by weight, and a gram of glucose and a gram of NaCl give different particle counts. Charge is irrelevant, since uncharged glucose contributes just as much as an ion.

cards.q: What is the osmolarity of a solution of 150 mM NaCl, assuming complete dissociation?
cards.a: 300 mOsm/L.
options: 150 mOsm/L
75 mOsm/L
300 mOsm/L
450 mOsm/L
cards.explanation: Each NaCl unit separates into one Na+ and one Cl-, so 150 mmol of NaCl yields 300 mmol of particles per liter. Using 150 counts the formula units rather than the particles they produce. Halving to 75 would be right only if two NaCl combined into one particle, which does not happen. Reaching 450 would require three particles per formula unit, as with CaCl2.

cards.q: Tonicity depends on the concentration of which solutes?
cards.a: Only the solutes that cannot cross the cell membrane.
options: All dissolved solutes, whether or not they can cross
Only the charged solutes in the solution
Only the solutes that the cell can metabolize
Only the solutes that cannot cross the cell membrane
cards.explanation: Tonicity predicts what a solution does to cell volume, and only impermeant solutes can hold water on one side, so penetrating solutes such as urea do not count. Counting every solute gives osmolarity, and confusing the two is the single most common error in this topic. Charge does not decide the issue, since impermeant glucose counts and permeant urea does not. Metabolism is a separate matter, although a solute that is consumed inside the cell behaves as if it were penetrating.

cards.q: What is the approximate osmolarity of normal human body fluids?
cards.a: About 300 mOsm/L.
options: About 300 mOsm/L
About 30 mOsm/L
About 1000 mOsm/L
About 150 mOsm/L
cards.explanation: Plasma, interstitial fluid, and intracellular fluid all sit near 300 mOsm/L, and that number is the reference point for calling a solution hyperosmotic or hyposmotic. A value near 30 would be close to distilled water and would lyse every cell. A thousand is nearer the concentrated urine of the kidney medulla, not general body fluid. The figure of 150 is the sodium concentration in millimoles per liter, which contributes about 300 mOsm/L once its accompanying anions are counted.

cards.q: What is the difference between osmolarity and osmolality?
cards.a: Osmolarity is particles per liter of solution and osmolality is particles per kilogram of water.
options: Osmolarity counts impermeant particles and osmolality counts all particles
Osmolarity is per liter of solution and osmolality is per kilogram of water
Osmolarity applies to plasma and osmolality applies to intracellular fluid
Osmolarity is measured at 37 C and osmolality is measured at 0 C
cards.explanation: The two differ only in the denominator, and in dilute body fluids the numbers are nearly identical, which is why the terms are often used interchangeably in physiology. The permeant versus impermeant distinction separates osmolarity from tonicity, not osmolarity from osmolality. Both terms apply to any fluid compartment. Neither term is tied to a particular temperature, although volume based osmolarity does shift slightly with temperature.

cards.q: In osmosis, which way does water move across a selectively permeable membrane?
cards.a: Toward the side with the higher concentration of impermeant solute.
options: Toward the side with the lower total solute concentration
Toward the side with the higher hydrostatic pressure
Toward the side with the higher concentration of impermeant solute
Equally in both directions with no net movement under any conditions
cards.explanation: Water follows solute, because the side with more solute particles has a lower water concentration, and water diffuses down its own gradient. Moving toward the more dilute side would be backward. Hydrostatic pressure pushes water away from the high pressure side, which is filtration rather than osmosis. Water does cross in both directions constantly, but the two fluxes are unequal whenever a solute gradient exists.

cards.q: Osmotic pressure of a solution is best described as what?
cards.a: The pressure that must be applied to stop net water movement into that solution.
options: The pressure the solution exerts on the walls of its container
The force with which solute particles push each other apart
The pressure generated by dissolved gases in the solution
The pressure needed to stop net water movement into the solution
cards.explanation: Osmotic pressure is defined by the opposing pressure needed to hold water back, and it rises as the number of impermeant particles rises. Pressure on the container wall is hydrostatic pressure, which is a separate quantity. Solute particles do not repel each other in any meaningful way here, since the effect is colligative and depends on number alone. Dissolved gas pressure is unrelated to osmosis.

cards.q: Tonicity is always stated relative to what?
cards.a: A cell, since it describes the solution's effect on cell volume.
options: A cell, since it describes the solution's effect on cell volume
Pure water, since that is the zero point of the scale
One liter of solution, since that is the standard volume
Plasma sodium, since sodium is the main extracellular ion
cards.explanation: Tonicity has no units and no meaning on its own, because it is a comparison: it tells you whether a cell placed in the solution will swell, shrink, or hold steady. Pure water is the reference for osmolarity being zero, not for tonicity. A liter is the volume basis for osmolarity. Sodium sets most of the extracellular osmolarity but is not the reference the term is defined against.

cards.q: What is the osmolarity of a 300 mM glucose solution?
cards.a: 300 mOsm/L.
options: 600 mOsm/L
300 mOsm/L
150 mOsm/L
900 mOsm/L
cards.explanation: Glucose does not dissociate, so each molecule contributes one particle and the millimolar and milliosmolar numbers are the same. Doubling to 600 would apply to a salt that splits into two ions, such as NaCl. Halving is never correct, since dissolving cannot reduce the particle count. Tripling would apply to a salt like CaCl2 that yields three ions.

cards.q: What is the osmolarity of a 100 mM CaCl2 solution, assuming complete dissociation?
cards.a: 300 mOsm/L.
options: 100 mOsm/L
200 mOsm/L
300 mOsm/L
400 mOsm/L
cards.explanation: Each CaCl2 unit gives one Ca2+ and two Cl-, so three particles per formula unit and 100 times 3 gives 300 mOsm/L. Using 100 counts formula units and ignores dissociation. Using 200 would be right for NaCl, which yields only two particles. The charge on calcium does not add a fourth particle, since osmolarity counts particles rather than charges.

cards.q: A solution contains 150 mM NaCl plus 100 mM glucose. What is its total osmolarity?
cards.a: 400 mOsm/L.
options: 250 mOsm/L
500 mOsm/L
350 mOsm/L
400 mOsm/L
cards.explanation: NaCl contributes 300 mOsm/L because it dissociates into two particles, and glucose contributes 100 mOsm/L because it does not dissociate, giving 400 mOsm/L in total. The value of 250 comes from adding the millimolar figures without doubling the salt. The value of 500 would come from doubling the glucose as well, which does not dissociate. The value of 350 mixes the two errors.

cards.q: A red blood cell with an internal osmolarity of 300 mOsm/L is placed in a 300 mOsm/L urea solution. Urea crosses the cell membrane. How is this solution best described?
cards.a: Isosmotic but hypotonic.
options: Isosmotic but hypotonic
Isosmotic and isotonic
Hyperosmotic and hypertonic
Hyposmotic and hypotonic
cards.explanation: The total particle count matches the cell, so the solution is isosmotic, but urea enters the cell and stops holding water outside, leaving an effective impermeant osmolarity of zero, so the cell swells and eventually lyses. Calling it isotonic treats urea as if it were trapped outside, which is the classic error. It is not hyperosmotic, because 300 equals 300. It is not hyposmotic either, since the measured osmolarity is normal, and only its tonicity is low.

cards.q: A cell of 300 mOsm/L is placed in a 400 mOsm/L NaCl solution. How is this solution described?
cards.a: Hyperosmotic and hypertonic.
options: Hyperosmotic but isotonic
Hyperosmotic and hypertonic
Isosmotic and isotonic
Hyperosmotic but hypotonic
cards.explanation: NaCl does not cross the membrane appreciably, so all 400 mOsm/L is effective and the solution both measures higher than the cell and pulls water out of it. A hyperosmotic solution is isotonic only when the excess above 300 is made of penetrating solute. It is not isosmotic, since 400 is not 300. It could be hypotonic only if its impermeant fraction were below 300, which it is not.

cards.q: A solution contains 300 mOsm/L NaCl plus 100 mOsm/L urea. A cell of 300 mOsm/L is placed in it. What is the correct description of the solution?
cards.a: Hyperosmotic but isotonic.
options: Hyperosmotic and hypertonic
Isosmotic and isotonic
Hyperosmotic but isotonic
Hyposmotic and hypotonic
cards.explanation: Total osmolarity is 400 mOsm/L, so the solution is hyperosmotic, but only the 300 mOsm/L of NaCl is impermeant, and 300 matches the cell, so after urea equilibrates the cell returns to its original volume. Calling it hypertonic counts the urea as if it were trapped outside. It is not isosmotic, since the measured total is 400. It is not hyposmotic in any sense, since both its total and its effective osmolarity are at or above the cell's.

cards.q: A solution contains 200 mOsm/L NaCl plus 200 mOsm/L urea. A cell of 300 mOsm/L is placed in it. How is this solution described?
cards.a: Hyperosmotic but hypotonic.
options: Hyperosmotic and hypertonic
Isosmotic but hypertonic
Hyposmotic and hypotonic
Hyperosmotic but hypotonic
cards.explanation: The total of 400 mOsm/L is above the cell, so the solution is hyperosmotic, but only the 200 mOsm/L of NaCl stays outside, and 200 is less than the cell's 300, so urea equilibrates and the cell ends up swollen. This is the case that shows most clearly that a hyperosmotic solution is not automatically hypertonic. It is not hypertonic, because its effective osmolarity is below the cell's. It is not isosmotic or hyposmotic, since its measured total is 400 mOsm/L.

cards.q: A cell with 300 mOsm/L of impermeant intracellular solute is placed in a solution of 200 mOsm/L NaCl plus 200 mOsm/L urea. Describe what happens to cell volume immediately and then after urea has equilibrated.
cards.a: The cell shrinks briefly, then swells past its original volume as urea enters and water follows.
options: The cell shrinks briefly, then swells past its original volume
The cell swells at once and keeps swelling, since the solution is hyposmotic
The cell shrinks and stays shrunken, since the solution measures 400 mOsm/L
The cell does not change volume at any point, since 400 is above 300
cards.explanation: Immediately the total osmolarity outside is 400 against 300 inside, so water leaves for a moment, but urea then diffuses into the cell down its gradient and water follows it, and since only 200 mOsm/L of impermeant solute remains outside against 300 inside, the cell finishes larger than it started. It does not swell from the first instant, because the initial total gradient favors water leaving. It does not stay shrunken, because urea does not stay outside. Volume certainly changes, in both directions at different times.

cards.q: Two patients each have a plasma osmolarity of 320 mOsm/L. In one it is raised by glucose that cannot enter most cells without insulin, and in the other by retained urea. Predict the effect on cell volume in each case.
cards.a: The glucose patient's cells shrink and the urea patient's cells stay near normal volume.
options: Both patients' cells shrink equally, since both have the same osmolarity
The glucose patient's cells shrink and the urea patient's cells stay near normal volume
The urea patient's cells shrink and the glucose patient's cells stay normal
Both patients' cells swell, since 320 is above the normal 300
cards.explanation: Glucose that cannot enter cells acts as an impermeant solute, so it raises both osmolarity and tonicity and draws water out of cells, while urea crosses membranes freely and equilibrates, raising osmolarity without raising tonicity. Equal osmolarity does not mean equal effect, which is exactly the point of separating the two terms. The comparison is not reversed, since urea is the penetrating solute here. Neither patient's cells swell, because neither plasma is hypotonic.

cards.q: A liter of 5 percent dextrose in water is infused. It is close to isosmotic in the bag, but the glucose is taken up by cells and metabolized. Predict the eventual effect on the tonicity of the extracellular fluid and on cell volume.
cards.a: The infusion ends up acting like pure water, so extracellular tonicity falls and cells swell.
options: It stays isotonic indefinitely, so cell volume is unchanged
It becomes hypertonic as glucose accumulates, so cells shrink
It ends up acting like pure water, so tonicity falls and cells swell
It stays entirely in the vascular space, so only blood volume changes
cards.explanation: Once the glucose is transported into cells and burned, the particles that made the solution isosmotic are gone, and what remains distributed through the body is free water, which dilutes the extracellular fluid and drives water into cells. It cannot stay isotonic, because that would require the glucose to stay outside the cells indefinitely. Glucose is consumed rather than accumulated, so the solution does not become hypertonic. Water distributes through all compartments rather than staying in the vessels, which is why isotonic saline and dextrose in water are used for different purposes.

cards.q: Cells placed in an unknown solution shrink within seconds, then return to exactly their original volume over the next several minutes. Glycerol crosses cell membranes slowly and NaCl does not. Which composition explains this result?
cards.a: 300 mOsm/L NaCl plus 100 mOsm/L glycerol, since glycerol slowly enters the cells.
options: 400 mOsm/L NaCl and no glycerol
200 mOsm/L NaCl plus 100 mOsm/L glycerol
300 mOsm/L NaCl and no glycerol
300 mOsm/L NaCl plus 100 mOsm/L glycerol
cards.explanation: The initial total of 400 mOsm/L pulls water out and the cell shrinks, and as glycerol crosses and equilibrates the effective impermeant osmolarity outside settles at 300, which matches the cell, so volume returns exactly to baseline. A pure 400 mOsm/L NaCl solution would leave the cell shrunken permanently, since none of it can enter. The 200 plus 100 mixture would leave only 200 mOsm/L impermeant outside, so the cell would end up swollen rather than back at baseline. A plain 300 mOsm/L NaCl solution would cause no shrinkage at all.

cards.q: During osmosis, which way does water move across a membrane that blocks the solute?
cards.a: Toward the side with more impermeant solute, where the water concentration is lower.
options: Toward the side with more impermeant solute
Toward the side with less impermeant solute
Toward the side with the higher hydrostatic pressure
Toward the warmer side of the membrane
cards.explanation: Water diffuses down its own concentration gradient, and adding solute lowers the water concentration, so water always moves toward the more concentrated side. Moving toward the dilute side would be backward and would concentrate that solution further. Hydrostatic pressure pushes water away from the high pressure side, which is filtration rather than osmosis. Temperature changes how fast osmosis happens but not which way water goes.

cards.q: What happens to a cell placed in a hypotonic solution?
cards.a: It swells.
options: It shrinks
It swells
Its volume does not change
It loses solute but keeps its volume
cards.explanation: Hypotonic means the effective impermeant solute outside is lower than inside, so water enters and the cell gains volume, and enough of it will burst a red blood cell. Shrinkage is the hypertonic result. No change is the isotonic result. Cells do lose some solute during volume regulation, but the immediate and defining response to a hypotonic solution is swelling.

cards.q: What happens to a cell placed in a hypertonic solution?
cards.a: It shrinks.
options: It swells
Its volume does not change
It shrinks
It bursts
cards.explanation: Hypertonic means more effective impermeant solute outside than inside, so water leaves the cell and it loses volume, which in a red blood cell is seen as crenation. Swelling and bursting are hypotonic results and require the opposite gradient. No change would require the two effective osmolarities to be equal.

cards.q: What happens to a cell placed in an isotonic solution?
cards.a: There is no net water movement and volume stays the same.
options: Water stops crossing the membrane entirely
Water moves in, then the cell pumps it back out
The cell slowly shrinks as solutes leak out
There is no net water movement and volume stays the same
cards.explanation: Isotonic means the effective impermeant osmolarity is equal on both sides, so water crosses in both directions at the same rate and volume holds steady. Water does not stop crossing, and the two way traffic continues constantly. No active pumping of water is involved, since there is no water pump. A steady leak of solutes is not what defines the isotonic case.

cards.q: Which membrane protein greatly increases the rate at which water crosses a cell membrane?
cards.a: Aquaporin.
options: Aquaporin
The Na+/K+ ATPase
GLUT4
The voltage gated Na+ channel
cards.explanation: Aquaporins are narrow channels that pass water in single file and exclude ions, and cells such as those of the kidney collecting duct insert them when water must move quickly. The Na+/K+ ATPase moves ions and sets up the gradients that water then follows, but it does not carry water. GLUT4 carries glucose. Voltage gated Na+ channels carry Na+ during an action potential.

cards.q: Which ion contributes most to the osmolarity of the intracellular fluid?
options: Na+
K+
Cl-
Ca2+
cards.explanation: Potassium is the dominant intracellular cation, and with the organic anions and proteins it accompanies, it accounts for most of the particles inside the cell. Na+ is the main extracellular cation and is kept low inside by the pump. Cl- is largely extracellular as well. Free intracellular Ca2+ is held near 0.0001 mM, far too low to affect osmolarity.

cards.q: Which ion contributes most to the osmolarity of the extracellular fluid?
cards.a: Na+.
options: K+
Ca2+
Na+
Mg2+
cards.explanation: Sodium and the anions that follow it make up most of the roughly 300 mOsm/L of extracellular fluid, which is why plasma sodium tracks so closely with plasma osmolarity. K+ is the main intracellular cation and sits near 4 mEq/L outside. Extracellular Ca2+ and Mg2+ are present at only a few milliequivalents per liter and contribute little to the total.

cards.q: When a cell has reached osmotic equilibrium with the fluid around it, how do intracellular and extracellular osmolarity compare?
cards.a: They are equal.
options: Intracellular osmolarity is higher
Extracellular osmolarity is higher
They vary independently, since the membrane separates them
They are equal
cards.explanation: Water crosses cell membranes easily, so it moves until the osmolarity on the two sides matches, and body fluids sit at roughly 300 mOsm/L everywhere at equilibrium. A permanent difference cannot be maintained, because water would keep moving until it was erased. That is true whichever side is imagined to be higher. The membrane blocks solutes, not water, so the two compartments are osmotically linked.

cards.q: A cell with an internal osmolarity of 300 mOsm/L is placed in 150 mOsm/L NaCl. Which way does water move, and what happens to the cell?
cards.a: Water enters and the cell swells.
options: Water enters and the cell swells
Water leaves and the cell shrinks
No net water movement occurs
Water enters and then leaves, so volume returns to normal
cards.explanation: The outside has fewer impermeant particles than the inside, so water moves toward the cell interior and volume rises. Water cannot leave, since that would require a higher effective osmolarity outside. There is a gradient here, so net movement occurs. Volume does not recover on its own in this case, because NaCl cannot enter the cell to erase the gradient.

cards.q: A cell with an internal osmolarity of 300 mOsm/L is placed in 600 mOsm/L NaCl. Predict the result.
cards.a: Water leaves and the cell shrinks.
options: Water enters and the cell swells
Water leaves and the cell shrinks
Volume is unchanged because NaCl cannot cross
NaCl enters until the two sides are equal
cards.explanation: With twice the impermeant solute outside, water moves out of the cell and the cell shrivels. Swelling would require the outside to be more dilute. The fact that NaCl cannot cross is precisely why the water gradient persists, so it does not protect volume. Sodium does leak slowly but is pumped back out, so it does not equilibrate the way urea does.

cards.q: A cell with an internal osmolarity of 300 mOsm/L is placed in 300 mOsm/L NaCl. What happens to cell volume?
cards.a: It stays the same.
options: It rises slowly as NaCl enters
It falls slowly as water leaves
It stays the same
It rises sharply and the cell lyses
cards.explanation: The impermeant solute concentrations match on the two sides, so water crosses equally in both directions and the cell holds its volume, which is why 0.9 percent NaCl is used as an intravenous fluid. NaCl does not flood in, since the pump keeps intracellular Na+ low. There is no gradient to draw water out. Lysis requires a hypotonic solution.

cards.q: A cell with an internal osmolarity of 300 mOsm/L is placed in a 300 mOsm/L urea solution. Predict what happens to cell volume.
cards.a: The cell swells, because urea enters the cell and no longer holds water outside.
options: Volume is unchanged, because the two osmolarities are equal
The cell shrinks, because urea pulls water out
Volume is unchanged, because urea cannot cross the membrane
The cell swells, because urea enters and stops holding water outside
cards.explanation: Urea crosses the membrane and equilibrates on both sides, so it stops contributing any osmotic pull, leaving the cell's own impermeant solutes to draw water in, and a red cell in this solution will lyse. Equal osmolarity is not enough, because tonicity depends only on the impermeant fraction. Urea cannot pull water out once it has equilibrated. Urea does cross, which is the whole reason this solution is hypotonic despite being isosmotic.

cards.q: A cell is given many extra aquaporins and then placed in a hypotonic solution. How does this change the outcome?
cards.a: The cell swells faster, but the final volume is the same.
options: The cell swells faster, but the final volume is the same
The cell swells to a larger final volume
The cell no longer swells, because aquaporins let solute escape
The cell shrinks instead, because water can now leave more easily
cards.explanation: Aquaporins change how quickly water moves, while the osmotic gradient decides how far it moves, so the endpoint is set by the solute concentrations and is unaffected. A larger endpoint would require a bigger gradient, which aquaporins do not create. Aquaporins pass water and exclude solute, so nothing escapes through them. Water moves both ways through aquaporins, and the net direction still follows the gradient, which favors entry here.

cards.q: A person becomes dehydrated and extracellular osmolarity rises from 300 to 320 mOsm/L. Predict the effect on intracellular volume.
cards.a: Water leaves the cells, so intracellular volume falls.
options: Water enters the cells, so intracellular volume rises
Water leaves the cells, so intracellular volume falls
Intracellular volume is unchanged, since the membrane blocks water
Intracellular volume rises, since the cells make more solute
cards.explanation: Losing water from the extracellular fluid concentrates the solutes left behind, so the extracellular fluid becomes hypertonic to the cells and water follows the gradient out of them, shrinking every compartment. Water cannot enter against that gradient. Cell membranes are highly permeable to water, so the intracellular compartment always shares in an osmotic disturbance. Brain cells do generate organic osmolytes over hours, but that is a slow adaptation and not the immediate result.

cards.q: A cell placed in a hypotonic solution doubles its volume. What has happened to its intracellular osmolarity?
cards.a: It has fallen to about half, because the same solute is dissolved in twice the water.
options: It has doubled, because the cell now holds twice as much fluid
It is unchanged, because osmolarity is a fixed property of the cell
It has fallen to about half, because the same solute is spread through twice the water
It has fallen to a quarter, because volume and osmolarity are squared terms
cards.explanation: The impermeant solutes cannot leave, so doubling the volume dilutes them to half their original concentration, and that dilution is what stops further water entry. Osmolarity cannot rise when water is added. It is not fixed, since it is a concentration and depends on the volume it is measured in. Osmolarity varies inversely with volume, with no squared relationship involved.

cards.q: A person drinks no water for a day and plasma osmolarity rises. Trace what happens to the extracellular and intracellular compartments once water has redistributed.
cards.a: Both compartments end up smaller and more concentrated, since water leaves the cells until the two osmolarities match.
options: Only the extracellular compartment shrinks, since cell membranes block water
The intracellular compartment shrinks while the extracellular compartment returns to its original volume
Both compartments end up larger, since cells release solute to hold water
Both compartments end up smaller and more concentrated, since water leaves cells until the osmolarities match
cards.explanation: Water is lost from the extracellular fluid first, which raises its osmolarity, and because water crosses cell membranes freely it then moves out of cells until both sides are equal, so both compartments lose volume and both end above 300 mOsm/L. The intracellular compartment cannot be spared, since membranes are permeable to water. The extracellular compartment gains some water back from the cells but does not return to its starting volume, since total body water has fallen. Neither compartment can grow when water is being lost from the body.

cards.q: Compare infusing one liter of isotonic saline with infusing one liter of pure water. Predict where each ends up and what happens to cell volume.
cards.a: Saline stays outside the cells and leaves their volume unchanged, while water spreads through all compartments and swells them.
options: Saline stays outside the cells while water spreads everywhere and swells them
Both stay extracellular, so neither changes cell volume
Both enter cells equally, so both swell the cells by the same amount
Saline enters cells and water stays extracellular, so saline swells the cells
cards.explanation: The Na+ in saline is held in the extracellular fluid by the pump, so it expands that compartment without creating an osmotic gradient across the cell membrane. Pure water adds no impermeant solute, so it dilutes the extracellular fluid and water then moves into cells until osmolarity is equal again. Saline cannot swell cells, because its solute cannot enter them. Water does not stay outside, because there is nothing holding it there.

cards.q: A cell placed in a hypotonic solution swells at first, then over the next twenty minutes returns partway toward its original size while still in the same solution. What accounts for the recovery?
cards.a: The cell exports K+, Cl-, and organic osmolytes, so water follows them out.
options: The cell pumps water back out using ATP
The cell exports K+, Cl-, and organic osmolytes, so water follows them out
The solution gradually becomes hypertonic on its own
The membrane becomes impermeable to water once the cell is stretched
cards.explanation: Since water cannot be moved directly, the only way for a cell to shed volume is to reduce its own impermeant solute content, and stretch activated channels release KCl and small organic solutes so water follows them out, a response called regulatory volume decrease. There is no ATP driven water pump anywhere in the body. The bathing solution is large and does not change measurably. Losing water permeability would freeze the cell at its swollen volume rather than shrink it.

cards.q: Cells are placed in two solutions that both measure 400 mOsm/L. Solution A is all NaCl. Solution B is 200 mOsm/L NaCl plus 200 mOsm/L glycerol, which slowly enters cells. Predict the final volume in each.
cards.a: Cells in A end up shrunken, while cells in B end up swollen above their original volume.
options: Both end up shrunken to the same degree, since both measure 400 mOsm/L
Cells in A end up swollen and cells in B end up shrunken
Cells in A end up shrunken, while cells in B end up swollen above their original volume
Both return to their original volume, since 400 mOsm/L is close to normal
cards.explanation: In A the entire 400 mOsm/L is impermeant, so water leaves and the cells stay shrunken, while in B only the 200 mOsm/L of NaCl stays outside, and once glycerol equilibrates that leaves 200 against the cell's 300, so water moves in and the cells finish larger than they started. Equal osmolarity does not predict equal volume change, because only impermeant solute counts. The pattern is not reversed, since it is B that contains the penetrating solute. Neither returns exactly to baseline, since neither effective osmolarity equals 300.

cards.q: In the diffusion and osmosis lab, dialysis tubing is used as a model of what?
cards.a: A selectively permeable membrane with pores of a fixed size.
options: A membrane that admits every solute equally
A membrane that actively pumps solutes across
A solid barrier that admits nothing
A selectively permeable membrane with pores of a fixed size
cards.explanation: Dialysis tubing lets small molecules through its pores and holds back large ones, which is why it models the size selectivity of a cell membrane. It is not freely permeable, since starch stays inside throughout the experiment. It has no proteins and no ATP, so it cannot pump anything. It is clearly not solid, since water and iodine cross it readily.

cards.q: Which indicator is used to detect starch, and what color change signals a positive result?
cards.a: Iodine solution, which turns from amber to blue black.
options: Iodine solution, which turns from amber to blue black
Benedict's reagent, which turns from blue to orange
Biuret reagent, which turns from blue to violet
Phenolphthalein, which turns from clear to pink
cards.explanation: Iodine slips into the coiled starch molecule and produces a deep blue black color, so any container that turns blue black contains starch.
